questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which statement best defines a gene?
options: A length of DNA that codes for a protein
A thread-like structure made of many chromosomes
A version of a characteristic shown in the phenotype
A type of cell found in the nucleus
questions.answer: A length of DNA that codes for a protein
questions.hint: Think about what a section of DNA is used to make.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is a chromosome?
options: A thread-like structure of DNA carrying genes
A protein made at a ribosome
questions.answer: A thread-like structure of DNA carrying genes
questions.hint: It is found in the nucleus and is much larger than a gene.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the term for an alternative form of a gene.
questions.hint: For example, the gene for eye colour can have different versions.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A human body cell contains 23 pairs of chromosomes. How many chromosomes is that in total?
questions.hint: Each pair contains two chromosomes.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: How many chromosomes are found in a normal human sperm cell?
questions.hint: Gametes contain one chromosome from each pair.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Where in an animal cell are chromosomes found?
questions.hint: It is the organelle that controls the cell.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four bases in DNA?
questions.hint: Three of these appear in DNA; one appears only in RNA.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: How does DNA control the protein made by a cell?
options: The sequence of bases determines the sequence of amino acids
The length of the chromosome determines the size of the cell
The number of genes determines the number of ribosomes
The shape of the nucleus determines the protein
questions.answer: The sequence of bases determines the sequence of amino acids
questions.hint: Think about order: bases in DNA, amino acids in a protein.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Name the molecule that carries a copy of a gene from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
questions.hint: It is a type of RNA whose name describes its job.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why must a copy of the gene leave the nucleus?
options: DNA stays in the nucleus but proteins are made at ribosomes in the cytoplasm
DNA is too small to be read in the nucleus
Amino acids are made in the nucleus
questions.answer: DNA stays in the nucleus but proteins are made at ribosomes in the cytoplasm
questions.hint: Compare where DNA is kept with where proteins are assembled.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Name the process in which a gene is copied into mRNA.
questions.hint: The name means 'writing across' into a new copy.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Name the process in which a ribosome uses mRNA to assemble a chain of amino acids.
questions.hint: The mRNA 'language' is turned into a protein 'language'.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Three bases code for one amino acid. How many bases are needed to code for a protein of 150 amino acids?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of amino acids by the bases per amino acid.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which is the correct order of events in protein synthesis?
options: Gene copied into mRNA → mRNA moves to ribosome → amino acids joined in order
mRNA moves to ribosome → gene copied → amino acids joined
Amino acids joined → mRNA made → gene copied
Ribosome copies DNA in the nucleus → protein leaves the cell
questions.answer: Gene copied into mRNA → mRNA moves to ribosome → amino acids joined in order
questions.hint: Start with what happens in the nucleus.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain why different body cells, such as muscle cells and nerve cells, can make different proteins even though they contain the same genes.
questions.hint: Think about whether every gene is used in every cell.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Describe how the information in a gene is used to make a specific protein. Refer to mRNA and ribosomes in your answer.
questions.hint: Follow the information from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, step by step.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual é o principal processo responsável por transformar a rocha-mãe em solo?
questions.hint: É o conjunto de ações do clima e dos seres vivos que desgastam a rocha.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama a rocha que dá origem a um solo?
questions.hint: Também é chamada de rocha matriz.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual tipo de intemperismo predomina em climas quentes e úmidos, como no Brasil tropical?
questions.hint: A água e o calor favorecem reações com os minerais.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual destes NÃO é um fator de formação dos solos?
questions.hint: Pense nos fatores que agem sobre a rocha ao longo do tempo.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chamam as camadas sobrepostas de um solo, vistas num corte vertical?
questions.hint: Elas recebem letras como O, A, B e C.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual horizonte do solo é mais rico em matéria orgânica?
questions.hint: É a camada mais superficial, com folhas e restos de seres vivos.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama a remoção de nutrientes do solo pela água da chuva que se infiltra?
questions.hint: A água 'lava' o solo de cima para baixo.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que caracteriza a laterização?
options: Concentração de óxidos de ferro e alumínio após intensa lixiviação, podendo formar uma crosta dura
Acúmulo de sal na superfície por irrigação
questions.answer: Concentração de óxidos de ferro e alumínio após intensa lixiviação, podendo formar uma crosta dura
questions.hint: Ocorre em climas tropicais com chuvas abundantes.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Que solo, de origem basáltica, é famoso pela fertilidade no Paraná e em São Paulo?
questions.hint: Sua cor avermelhada vem do ferro.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama a erosão profunda e de grandes dimensões que forma enormes buracos no terreno?
questions.hint: É uma etapa mais grave que o sulco e a ravina.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual é a ordem correta de agravamento da erosão causada pela água que escorre?
questions.hint: Comece pela marca mais rasa.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual é uma consequência da erosão para os rios?
questions.hint: Os sedimentos do solo vão parar no leito do rio.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual técnica agrícola ajuda a reduzir a erosão em terrenos inclinados?
questions.hint: As fileiras acompanham a mesma altitude e freiam a água.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: A desertificação, segundo a definição usada pela ONU, ocorre principalmente em áreas:
questions.hint: No Brasil, ela preocupa sobretudo o Sertão nordestino.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que o processo do sudoeste do Rio Grande do Sul é chamado de arenização, e não de desertificação?
options: Porque ocorre em clima úmido, sem aridez
Porque não há areia na região
questions.answer: Porque ocorre em clima úmido, sem aridez
questions.hint: Compare o clima da região com o das áreas semiáridas.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique como o desmatamento e o manejo inadequado do solo podem levar à desertificação no semiárido brasileiro e indique uma medida para combatê-la.
questions.hint: Pense na cobertura vegetal, na erosão e no uso do solo e da água.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What does a statement of financial position show?
options: A business's assets, liabilities and equity at a particular date
A business's sales and costs over a year
Only the cash coming in and out of a business
The wages paid to each employee
questions.answer: A business's assets, liabilities and equity at a particular date
questions.hint: It is often described as a snapshot.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the term for items of value that a business owns.
questions.hint: Machinery and inventory are examples.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the term for debts that a business owes.
questions.hint: Loans and money owed to suppliers are examples.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is a non-current asset?
questions.hint: Non-current assets are kept for more than one year.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is a current asset?
questions.hint: Current assets are likely to be turned into cash within a year.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is a current liability?
questions.hint: Current liabilities must be paid within a year.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Money owed to a business by its customers is called:
questions.hint: The business will receive this money.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is a non-current liability?
options: A bank loan repayable over ten years
questions.answer: A bank loan repayable over ten years
questions.hint: Look for a debt that lasts more than one year.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has total assets of $480,000 and total liabilities of $190,000. Calculate its net assets in $.
questions.hint: Net assets = total assets − total liabilities.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: On a statement of financial position, net assets are equal to:
questions.hint: The statement must balance.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A shop has current assets of $36,000 and current liabilities of $24,000. Calculate its working capital in $.
questions.hint: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A firm has current assets of $50,000 and current liabilities of $25,000. Calculate its current ratio.
questions.hint: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A current ratio well below 1 most likely suggests that a business:
options: May struggle to pay its short-term debts
questions.answer: May struggle to pay its short-term debts
questions.hint: Compare what it owns in the short term with what it owes.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which group would be MOST interested in a statement of financial position before lending money?
questions.hint: Think about who wants to know if a loan can be repaid.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain one limitation of using a statement of financial position to judge how well a business is performing.
questions.hint: Think about what the statement does not show, and when it was drawn up.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A company's inventory has risen sharply while its cash has fallen. Analyse what this might mean for the business.
questions.hint: Consider liquidity and whether the inventory can be sold.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What does 'unsaturated' mean when describing an alkene?
options: It contains a carbon–carbon double bond
questions.answer: It contains a carbon–carbon double bond
questions.hint: Think about the bond that makes alkenes different from alkanes.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
questions.hint: Ethene is C2H4.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Give the molecular formula of propene.
questions.hint: Use the general formula with n = 3.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which statement best describes cracking?
options: Breaking down large alkane molecules into smaller, more useful molecules
Joining small alkenes to make polymers
Separating crude oil by boiling point
questions.answer: Breaking down large alkane molecules into smaller, more useful molecules
questions.hint: The word suggests molecules being split.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which conditions are used in catalytic cracking?
options: Low temperature and high pressure only
questions.hint: The name 'catalytic' gives one clue.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which products are formed by cracking a large alkane?
options: Smaller alkanes, alkenes and sometimes hydrogen
questions.answer: Smaller alkanes, alkenes and sometimes hydrogen
questions.hint: Cracking produces a mixture.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Decane is cracked: C10H22 → C8H18 + X. Give the formula of X.
questions.hint: Balance the carbon and hydrogen atoms.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Give one reason why oil refineries crack long-chain alkanes.
options: There is more demand for shorter-chain fuels like petrol than supply
Shorter alkanes are cheaper to store
questions.answer: There is more demand for shorter-chain fuels like petrol than supply
questions.hint: Compare supply and demand for different fractions.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What colour change is seen when an alkene is shaken with bromine water?
questions.hint: The bromine is used up in a reaction.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is seen when an alkane is shaken with bromine water at room temperature in the dark?
questions.hint: Alkanes are saturated.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What type of reaction occurs when bromine reacts with ethene?
questions.hint: Two molecules join to make one product.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Name the product formed when ethene reacts with bromine.
questions.hint: Two bromine atoms add across the double bond of a two-carbon molecule.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Name the product when ethene reacts with hydrogen.
questions.hint: The alkene becomes the matching alkane.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Name the product made when ethene reacts with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst.
questions.hint: It is an alcohol with two carbon atoms.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of ethene, C2H4. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
questions.hint: Add the masses of all the atoms.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Describe how bromine water can be used to distinguish between hexane and hexene, and explain the difference in terms of bonding.
questions.hint: Mention the observations for each and the double bond.

comp.topic: Writing a complete solution to a scenario problem

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In a 15-mark scenario question, what should you do first?
options: Identify the inputs, processes and outputs in the scenario
Write the validation last without planning
questions.answer: Identify the inputs, processes and outputs in the scenario
questions.hint: Think about what the program receives and what it must produce.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A scenario says data for 30 students must be stored and later searched. Which data structure is most suitable?
questions.hint: You need many values of the same type under one name.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which loop is best for repeating an input until the user enters a valid value?
options: A count-controlled FOR loop with fixed steps
questions.hint: You do not know in advance how many attempts will be needed.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A mark must be a whole number from 0 to 100. Which validation check is this mainly?
questions.hint: It checks between a lower and an upper limit.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: State the name of the validation check that makes sure a field has not been left empty.
questions.hint: The data must be present.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A scenario requires a fixed number of 7 days to be processed. Which loop is most appropriate?
questions.hint: The number of repetitions is known before the loop starts.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What term describes a variable used to add up values inside a loop, starting at 0?
questions.hint: Its value grows each time round the loop.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: To find the highest value in an array, what should the variable Highest be set to before the loop?
options: The first element of the array (or a value lower than any possible data)
The last index of the array
Zero in every case, even if values can be negative
questions.answer: The first element of the array (or a value lower than any possible data)
questions.hint: Every real value must be able to replace it.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: An array holds the values 12, 7, 19, 4, 8. A program calculates the average. What is the output?
questions.hint: Add all five values, then divide.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Why is it good practice to use meaningful identifiers such as TotalScore in a scenario answer?
options: They make the program easier to read and maintain
They make the program run faster
They are required for the program to compile
questions.answer: They make the program easier to read and maintain
questions.hint: Think about the examiner or another programmer reading your code.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In pseudocode, which statement correctly checks if a value is outside the range 1 to 50?
questions.hint: A number cannot be both below 1 and above 50 at once.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Two arrays, Names[] and Scores[], store data so that the same index refers to the same student. What are these called?
questions.hint: They run side by side.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A loop runs FOR Count ← 1 TO 5 and adds Count × 2 to Total, which starts at 0. What is Total at the end?
questions.hint: Work out 2 + 4 + 6 + …

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A scenario asks you to output the name of the student with the lowest score. Which extra variable is most useful?
options: One that stores the index of the current lowest score
One that stores the length of each name
One that counts how many inputs were invalid
questions.answer: One that stores the index of the current lowest score
questions.hint: The index links the score back to the name.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain why a scenario solution should include comments and an output message for invalid input.
questions.hint: Think about the user and anyone marking or maintaining the program.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A program must store the daily temperatures for one week, reject values below -30 or above 50, and output the average and the hottest day. Describe the main steps your solution would take.
questions.hint: Mention data structure, loop, validation, totals and finding a maximum.

econ.topic: Economic data skills: tables, graphs and percentage changes

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is the formula for percentage change?
questions.hint: Always divide by the starting value.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A country's exports rise from $200 billion to $230 billion. Calculate the percentage change.
questions.hint: Find the change first, then divide by the original.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The price of a good falls from $50 to $40. Calculate the percentage change (give a negative number for a fall).
questions.hint: The change is negative.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: In an index number series, what value is the base year given?
questions.hint: Other years are compared with it.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Using 2020 as the base year (index 100), output rises from 400 units in 2020 to 460 units in 2022. What is the index number for 2022?
questions.hint: Divide 2022 by 2020 and multiply by 100.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A price index rises from 120 to 132. Calculate the percentage increase in prices.
questions.hint: Index points are not the same as a percentage change.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A price index moves from 100 to 108. What does this show?
options: Prices rose by 8% since the base year
questions.answer: Prices rose by 8% since the base year
questions.hint: An index measures relative change, not actual prices.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 3%. What has happened to the price level?
options: It is still rising, but more slowly
questions.answer: It is still rising, but more slowly
questions.hint: Positive inflation always means prices are going up.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What one-word term describes the general direction in which data moves over time?
questions.hint: It ignores small ups and downs.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Unemployment rises from 4% to 5% of the labour force. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 1 percentage point, which is a 25% increase
questions.answer: It rose by 1 percentage point, which is a 25% increase
questions.hint: Compare the difference with the percentage change.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Real GDP rises by 2% a year from $500 billion. What is real GDP after one year, in $ billion?
questions.hint: Find 2% of 500.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Why do economists use real rather than nominal GDP when comparing years?
options: Real GDP removes the effect of inflation
questions.answer: Real GDP removes the effect of inflation
questions.hint: Think about whether rising prices make output look bigger.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A table shows GDP per head for four countries. Which conclusion is safest?
options: It shows average income, not how income is shared
It shows exactly how rich every citizen is
It measures the quality of life completely
questions.answer: It shows average income, not how income is shared
questions.hint: An average can hide inequality.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A firm's revenue was $80,000 one year and $60,000 the next. Calculate the percentage change (negative for a fall).
questions.hint: Divide the change by 80,000.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A graph shows a country's inflation rate falling from 9% to 4% over three years. Explain what this tells you about prices and why it could still be a problem for consumers.
questions.hint: Think about the price level versus the rate of change.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Explain one limitation of using a single year's data to judge whether an economy is performing well.
questions.hint: Consider trends, one-off events and other indicators.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In a descriptive composition, what is the main purpose?
options: To create a vivid picture and atmosphere for the reader
To tell a story with a clear plot twist
To persuade the reader to change their mind
questions.answer: To create a vivid picture and atmosphere for the reader
questions.hint: Focus on what is seen, heard and felt.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: How long is a sensible planning time for a 350–450 word timed composition?
questions.hint: Enough to organise ideas but leave time to write and check.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which plan structure works well for a descriptive piece?
options: Moving through a place or a period of time, focusing on a different detail in each paragraph
A list of facts in bullet points
questions.answer: Moving through a place or a period of time, focusing on a different detail in each paragraph
questions.hint: Think of a camera moving or the light changing.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sense is used in this sentence: "The air tasted of salt and diesel."?
questions.hint: Look at the verb.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence uses personification?
options: The old house groaned in the wind.
The house was as cold as ice.
questions.answer: The old house groaned in the wind.
questions.hint: Which one gives a human action to an object?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which is the best example of a precise verb in descriptive writing?
options: The leaves skittered across the path.
The leaves went across the path.
The leaves moved across the path.
The leaves were across the path.
questions.answer: The leaves skittered across the path.
questions.hint: Choose the verb that shows exactly how they moved.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What literary term describes a comparison using "like" or "as"?
questions.hint: It is not a metaphor.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Why should a descriptive composition avoid too much plot?
options: Action can take over and the description of atmosphere is lost
Plot is not allowed in exams
It makes the piece too short
questions.answer: Action can take over and the description of atmosphere is lost
questions.hint: The marks reward description, not events.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence uses a short sentence for effect most successfully?
options: The market was very busy and noisy and full of people.
I went to the market on a Saturday morning with my aunt.
There were many stalls selling many different things.
questions.hint: Brevity can create contrast and tension.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which opening is most effective for a description titled "The Station at Midnight"?
options: Under a single flickering bulb, the empty platform held its breath.
I am going to describe a station at midnight.
Once upon a time there was a station.
Stations are places where trains stop.
questions.answer: Under a single flickering bulb, the empty platform held its breath.
questions.hint: Look for imagery and atmosphere from the first line.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What term means using the same initial consonant sound in nearby words, as in "silent, silver sand"?
questions.hint: Listen to the beginnings of the words.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What does "varying sentence openings" mean?
options: Starting sentences in different ways, e.g. with an adverb, a verb or a prepositional phrase
Writing every sentence the same length
questions.answer: Starting sentences in different ways, e.g. with an adverb, a verb or a prepositional phrase
questions.hint: Think about how sentences begin.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In the last 5 minutes of a timed composition, what is the best use of time?
options: Proofreading for spelling, punctuation and repeated words
questions.answer: Proofreading for spelling, punctuation and repeated words
questions.hint: Accuracy is part of the mark.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which ending is most effective for a descriptive piece that began at dawn on a beach?
options: As the sun dropped behind the dunes, the sand gave back the day's warmth to the dark.
And then I woke up and it was all a dream.
That is my description of the beach.
questions.answer: As the sun dropped behind the dunes, the sand gave back the day's warmth to the dark.
questions.hint: A circular structure echoes the opening.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Write a plan of five paragraph focuses for a descriptive composition titled "A Busy Kitchen".
questions.hint: Use the senses and move through time or space.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Write two sentences describing a storm approaching a city, using at least one metaphor and one varied sentence opening.
questions.hint: Choose precise verbs and imagery.

en_lit.topic: Coursework option: comparing two complete texts (about 1,500 words)

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the main focus of a comparative coursework essay?
options: How the two texts are similar and different in ideas, methods and effects
A retelling of the plot of each text
Listing every quotation you can find
questions.answer: How the two texts are similar and different in ideas, methods and effects
questions.hint: Think about "compare" as the key command word.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the approximate word limit for this coursework option?
questions.hint: It is stated in the task title.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which is the best way to structure a comparative essay?
options: Integrate both texts in each paragraph around a shared point
Write all about text A, then all about text B, with no links
Write only about the drama text
Put all quotations in a list at the end
questions.answer: Integrate both texts in each paragraph around a shared point
questions.hint: Comparison should be ongoing, not left to the end.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What word describes instructions in a play script telling actors how to move or speak?
questions.hint: They are not spoken aloud.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: When writing about a drama text, what should you always consider?
options: How the play would work on stage for an audience
Only the length of each act
questions.answer: How the play would work on stage for an audience
questions.hint: Plays are written to be performed.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which phrase is most useful for showing a difference between two texts?
questions.hint: Choose the connective that signals difference.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which phrase is most useful for showing a similarity?
questions.hint: Choose the connective that signals sameness.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What term describes weaving short quotations into your own sentences?
questions.hint: The quotation becomes part of your sentence.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which sentence integrates evidence most effectively?
options: The character's description of the sea as "a grey cage" suggests that she feels trapped.
She says something about the sea. "A grey cage".
The sea is mentioned on page 12.
questions.answer: The character's description of the sea as "a grey cage" suggests that she feels trapped.
questions.hint: Look for a quotation inside an analytical sentence.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What does a dramatic monologue or soliloquy allow the audience to learn?
options: A character's private thoughts and feelings
The exact time and date of the action
questions.answer: A character's private thoughts and feelings
questions.hint: Think about one character speaking alone.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the name for the point in a play when the audience knows something a character does not?
questions.hint: It creates tension for the audience.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Why is a thesis statement important in the introduction?
options: It sets out the main line of argument that the essay will compare
It summarises the plot of both texts
It lists every technique you will mention
It is not needed in coursework
questions.answer: It sets out the main line of argument that the essay will compare
questions.hint: The essay should prove something.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the best use of a first draft in coursework?
options: To develop ideas and get feedback before refining
To submit straight away as the final version
To copy notes from a study guide
questions.answer: To develop ideas and get feedback before refining
questions.hint: Drafting is a process.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which is the strongest comparative topic sentence?
options: Both texts present isolation, but the play shows it through silence on stage while the novel uses inner thoughts.
questions.answer: Both texts present isolation, but the play shows it through silence on stage while the novel uses inner thoughts.
questions.hint: Look for a shared idea plus a difference in method.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain why it is important to write about the writers' methods, not only the themes, in a comparative essay.
questions.hint: Think about how meaning is created.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Write a short comparative paragraph plan (point, evidence from both texts, comparison) on how two texts present conflict between generations.
questions.hint: You can use invented short quotations to show the structure.

chapters.title: Capítulo 1: A caixa do depósito
chapters.synopsis: Lia, de dezesseis anos, ajuda a tia restauradora num museu de Salvador e encontra um caderno do século XVII com um poema cheio de contrastes.
chapters.text:
Lia tinha prometido a si mesma que aquelas férias seriam de praia e preguiça. Mas a tia Celeste, restauradora do pequeno Museu do Largo, em Salvador, precisava de ajuda para organizar um depósito que ninguém abria havia décadas, e Lia, sem saber dizer não, acabou trocando o mar por caixas empoeiradas.
O depósito ficava no andar de cima, debaixo de um telhado que estalava com o calor. Havia santos sem braço, molduras sem quadro e baús com cheiro de cera velha. A tia andava entre tudo aquilo como quem visita parentes queridos. Lia só pensava no ventilador quebrado.
No fundo de um baú, embrulhado num pano roxo, estava um caderno de capa de couro. As páginas, amareladas e grossas, eram cobertas por uma letra inclinada, cheia de voltas. Na primeira folha, alguém tinha escrito: "Versos de Frei Anselmo do Desterro, ano de 1680".
— Tia, olha isto — chamou Lia, quase sem respirar.
Celeste calçou as luvas brancas e pegou o caderno com cuidado. Seus olhos brilharam.
— Isto é do século dezessete, Lia. Do tempo do Barroco.
Lia sabia pouco sobre o Barroco: lembrava de igrejas cheias de ouro e de uma aula sonolenta numa sexta-feira. A tia, porém, explicou com entusiasmo que aquele era um tempo de muitas dúvidas. A Igreja Católica, depois da Reforma Protestante, tinha reagido com a Contrarreforma, tentando reconquistar os fiéis. As pessoas viviam divididas entre o medo do pecado e a vontade de aproveitar a vida, entre o céu prometido e a terra cheia de prazeres.
— E essa divisão aparece na escrita — completou a tia. — Leia o primeiro poema.
Lia leu em voz baixa:
"Sou luz que em sombra vive escondida,
Sou fogo que no gelo se consome;
Busco o céu, mas a terra tem meu nome,
E morro um pouco a cada dia de vida."
Ela ficou em silêncio. Os versos pareciam brigar uns com os outros: luz e sombra, fogo e gelo, céu e terra.
— Ele junta coisas opostas o tempo todo — disse Lia.
— Isso tem nome: antítese — respondeu Celeste. — É a figura preferida dos poetas barrocos. Eles não conseguiam escolher um lado, então escreviam sobre os dois ao mesmo tempo.
Naquela tarde, o calor continuou insuportável e o ventilador continuou quebrado. Mas, quando desceu as escadas, Lia levava o caderno abraçado ao peito, como se fosse ela quem o tivesse escrito. Pela primeira vez nas férias, estava curiosa por alguma coisa.
À noite, antes de dormir, escreveu no celular uma frase só para si: "Quero entender esse frei que vivia entre a luz e a sombra." Depois apagou a luz e, no escuro, ficou repetindo o último verso até pegar no sono.

chapters.title: Capítulo 2: Ouro e escuridão
chapters.synopsis: Lia visita uma igreja barroca com a tia e entende como a arte da Contrarreforma queria emocionar e convencer os fiéis.
chapters.text:
No sábado, a tia Celeste levou Lia a uma igreja antiga perto do museu. Por fora, a fachada era cinzenta e manchada pela chuva. Lia achou que seria uma visita rápida e sem graça.
Quando as portas se abriram, porém, ela parou na entrada. As paredes pareciam feitas de ouro. Colunas retorcidas subiam até o teto, cobertas de folhas, frutas e anjinhos esculpidos em madeira dourada. No alto, uma pintura mostrava nuvens que se abriam para um céu luminoso, enquanto, nos cantos, figuras se escondiam numa penumbra pesada.
— Parece que o teto vai cair em cima da gente — sussurrou Lia.
— Essa era a ideia — riu a tia. — Ou quase. A arte barroca queria impressionar. Depois da Reforma, a Igreja percebeu que precisava tocar o coração das pessoas, não só a razão. Então encheu as igrejas de brilho, movimento e drama.
Elas andaram devagar pela nave. Lia notou que nada ali era calmo: os santos tinham os olhos voltados para cima, as mãos abertas, as roupas esvoaçando como se houvesse vento dentro da igreja. Até as colunas pareciam se torcer.
Perto do altar, um raio de sol atravessava uma janela alta e iluminava apenas o rosto de uma imagem, deixando o resto no escuro.
— Isso se chama claro-escuro — explicou Celeste. — É o contraste forte entre luz e sombra. Os pintores barrocos usavam muito.
Lia lembrou imediatamente do poema do frei.
— É igual ao poema, tia! Luz que em sombra vive escondida.
— Exatamente. A pintura, a arquitetura e a poesia do Barroco falavam a mesma língua. Todas mostravam o ser humano dividido, puxado ao mesmo tempo para o alto e para baixo.
Sentaram-se num banco de madeira. Lia abriu o caderno, que agora andava sempre com ela, protegido num envelope de papel especial. Na terceira página, encontrou um poema curto que parecia descrever aquela mesma igreja:
"Entre o ouro que ao céu me chama
E a sombra onde o pecado mora,
Minha alma ri e minha alma chora,
E é gelo o que no peito inflama."
Ela leu duas vezes. Depois olhou ao redor, para o ouro, para as sombras, para os santos com os olhos no teto.
— Ele devia sentar aqui, igual a gente — disse baixinho.
— Talvez não aqui, mas num lugar muito parecido — respondeu a tia. — Os artistas daquele tempo queriam que o fiel saísse da igreja comovido, com vontade de mudar de vida.
Na saída, a fachada cinzenta pareceu diferente a Lia. Agora ela sabia que era só uma casca, como se a igreja guardasse um segredo luminoso por dentro. Ao atravessar a rua, ela pensou que talvez as pessoas também fossem assim: simples por fora, cheias de contrastes por dentro.
Naquela noite, mandou uma mensagem para os amigos Bia e Tomás: "Encontrei um poeta de trezentos anos. Vocês precisam conhecer." Nenhum dos dois entendeu nada, mas ambos responderam que iriam ao museu na segunda.

chapters.title: Capítulo 3: O poema que parecia um labirinto
chapters.synopsis: Bia se encanta com um poema rebuscado do caderno, e a tia explica o cultismo, o jogo de palavras e de imagens.
chapters.text:
Na segunda-feira, Bia e Tomás chegaram ao museu com cara de quem esperava uma brincadeira. Bia trazia um caderno de desenhos debaixo do braço; Tomás, como sempre, uma calculadora no bolso, embora ninguém soubesse para quê.
Celeste mostrou o caderno do frei numa mesa iluminada. Bia se debruçou sobre as páginas e apontou um poema longo, cheio de palavras difíceis.
— Esse aqui parece um labirinto — disse ela, encantada.
Lia leu em voz alta:
"Do sol a rubra coroa, que ao mar desmaia,
Em nácar se desfaz, em ouro se derrama;
E a tarde, de cristal vestida, à praia
Tece de púrpura a sua última chama."
Tomás franziu a testa.
— Eu li três vezes e ainda não sei o que aconteceu.
— Aconteceu um pôr do sol — respondeu Bia, rindo. — Só que ele não diz isso de jeito simples. Ele chama o sol de "rubra coroa", a tarde fica "de cristal vestida". É como se cada palavra fosse uma joia.
A tia aprovou com a cabeça.
— Bia descobriu sozinha o que se chama cultismo. É uma tendência do Barroco que valoriza a forma: muitas metáforas, palavras raras, sons bonitos e frases com a ordem invertida.
— Ordem invertida? — perguntou Tomás.
— Veja o primeiro verso: "Do sol a rubra coroa". Na ordem direta, seria "a rubra coroa do sol". Essa inversão tem nome: hipérbato.
Tomás pegou um papel e começou a reescrever o poema na ordem direta, como se resolvesse uma equação. Bia, ao contrário, desenhava o pôr do sol com lápis de cor: laranja, roxo, dourado.
— Para mim, fica mais bonito do jeito difícil — disse ela. — Dá vontade de ver as cores.
— Para mim, fica mais claro do jeito fácil — rebateu Tomás.
Lia observava os dois discutindo e pensou que a briga deles era muito barroca: um puxava para a razão, o outro para os sentidos.
— Os poetas cultistas queriam exatamente isso que a Bia sentiu — explicou Celeste. — Criar imagens que encham os olhos, quase como uma pintura feita de palavras. Às vezes exageravam tanto que o leitor se perdia, e por isso alguns críticos da época reclamavam.
No fim da tarde, Tomás mostrou sua versão: "O sol vermelho se põe no mar e a tarde deixa a praia colorida." Todos riram, porque estava correta, mas tinha perdido toda a magia.
— Viu? — disse Bia. — O sentido é o mesmo, mas o efeito não.
Tomás guardou a calculadora, derrotado, mas com um meio sorriso.
— Tudo bem. Mas aposto que esse frei também sabia escrever com lógica. Amanhã eu acho a prova.
Lia fechou o caderno com cuidado. Gostava cada vez mais daquele frei que, trezentos anos antes, já fazia os amigos discutirem.

chapters.title: Capítulo 4: O sermão da ampulheta
chapters.synopsis: Tomás encontra no caderno um sermão com raciocínio em cadeia e descobre o conceptismo, o jogo de ideias.
chapters.text:
Tomás chegou ao museu antes de todo mundo. Quando Lia e Bia entraram, ele já estava sentado à mesa, com as luvas brancas, folheando o caderno com uma concentração assustadora.
— Achei! — anunciou, sem nem dizer bom-dia. — Não é poema. É um sermão.
Na metade do caderno, a letra do frei mudava: ficava mais apertada, como se ele escrevesse com pressa. O título dizia "Sermão da Ampulheta". Tomás leu em voz alta, devagar:
"Dizeis que tendes tempo. E o que é o tempo senão areia que cai? Se é areia, escorre; se escorre, acaba; se acaba, não é vosso. Logo, o tempo que dizeis ter, já o estais perdendo enquanto o dizeis. E se o perdeis falando, por que não o ganhais mudando?"
Bia ficou um instante calada.
— Isso é quase uma equação — admitiu.
— Eu disse! — Tomás bateu na mesa, satisfeito. — Olha como ele pensa: o tempo é areia, areia escorre, o que escorre acaba. Uma ideia puxa a outra até chegar a uma conclusão que pega o ouvinte de surpresa.
A tia Celeste, que examinava uma moldura ali perto, aproximou-se.
— Tomás encontrou o outro lado do Barroco: o conceptismo. Enquanto o cultismo brinca com a forma, o conceptismo brinca com as ideias. Usa raciocínios engenhosos, comparações inesperadas, argumentos em cadeia. E o sermão era o lugar perfeito para isso, porque o padre precisava convencer os fiéis.
— Então o cultismo é para os olhos e o conceptismo é para a cabeça? — perguntou Lia.
— É uma boa maneira de lembrar — sorriu a tia. — Mas muitos autores usavam os dois.
Bia releu a última frase do sermão: "E se o perdeis falando, por que não o ganhais mudando?"
— Ele também brinca com as palavras aqui: perder e ganhar, falando e mudando.
— Viu? Antítese de novo — disse Lia. — Esse frei não larga as antíteses.
Tomás, empolgado, resolveu testar o método. Pegou um papel e escreveu um "sermão" sobre o celular: "Dizes que o celular te aproxima dos amigos. Se aproxima os de longe, afasta os de perto; se afasta os de perto, deixa-te sozinho; logo, o que te une é o mesmo que te separa."
As meninas aplaudiram, e ele ficou vermelho.
— Você acabou de escrever um texto conceptista — disse Celeste. — Daqui a trezentos anos alguém vai encontrar isso num baú.
Todos riram. Mas Lia percebeu que o sermão tinha deixado uma pergunta no ar. Se o tempo escorria como areia, o que o frei teria feito com o tempo dele? Quem tinha sido aquele homem, além das palavras?
Antes de ir embora, ela virou com cuidado a última página escrita do caderno. Ali havia apenas uma rosa seca, achatada entre as folhas, e uma frase pequena: "Para quem chegar depois."
Lia sentiu um arrepio. Pela primeira vez, o caderno parecia uma mensagem endereçada a alguém.

chapters.title: Capítulo 5: A rosa da manhã
chapters.synopsis: A rosa seca leva Lia a um poema sobre a brevidade da vida, e os amigos discutem a ideia de aproveitar o tempo.
chapters.text:
A rosa seca não saiu da cabeça de Lia. No dia seguinte, ela pediu à tia para examinar a página com uma lupa. Sob a flor, quase apagado, havia um poema que ninguém tinha notado antes.
"Ontem, rosa, eras rubra e orgulhosa,
De orvalho coroada, a manhã te amava;
Hoje és pó que o vento leva e lava,
Lição muda, mas sábia e piedosa.
Ó tu, que lês, não sejas preguiçosa:
Se a flor que hoje sorri, amanhã finda,
Colhe da vida a hora breve e linda,
Antes que a tarde a deixe sem a rosa."
— Ele está falando da rosa, mas não é só da rosa — disse Bia, que já tinha aprendido a desconfiar dos poemas.
— É da vida — completou Lia. — A rosa nasce bonita de manhã e à tarde já murchou. Como a gente.
Celeste explicou que aquele era um dos temas mais fortes do Barroco: a fugacidade, ou seja, a rapidez com que tudo passa — a beleza, a juventude, a própria vida. Muitos poetas usavam a imagem da flor, da vela que se apaga, da sombra que foge.
— E esse "colhe da vida a hora breve" lembra uma ideia antiga, que vem dos poetas latinos: o carpe diem, "aproveita o dia".
Tomás cruzou os braços.
— Mas espera. No sermão, o frei mandava a gente mudar de vida e pensar na alma. Agora ele diz para aproveitar a vida? Ele não se decide?
Houve um silêncio. Lia achou que Tomás tinha razão, mas também achou que não era bem uma contradição.
— Talvez seja isso mesmo — disse ela, devagar. — Ele vivia dividido. Queria o céu e gostava da terra. Tinha medo do tempo e queria aproveitar o tempo. O Barroco é isso, não é, tia?
— É exatamente isso — respondeu Celeste. — O homem barroco sente as duas coisas ao mesmo tempo. A consciência de que a vida é curta pode levar alguém a buscar a fé ou a buscar o prazer. Às vezes, as duas coisas no mesmo poema.
Bia desenhou a rosa duas vezes: uma vermelha e aberta, outra cinza e curvada. Colocou os desenhos lado a lado.
— Uma antítese em desenho — disse, orgulhosa.
No fim da tarde, Lia ficou sozinha com a página. Pensou nas férias que tinha imaginado de praia e preguiça, e em como tinha quase desperdiçado aqueles dias reclamando do calor. Pensou na avó, que sempre dizia que os anos passam mais rápido do que os dias.
Fechou o caderno, guardou-o no envelope e decidiu fazer uma coisa que não fazia havia muito tempo: voltou para casa a pé, pela orla, olhando o pôr do sol do começo ao fim, sem tirar nenhuma foto.
Quando o último pedaço de sol sumiu no mar, ela lembrou do poema de Bia, da "rubra coroa" que ao mar desmaia, e sorriu. Pela primeira vez, a poesia e a vida pareciam a mesma coisa.

chapters.title: Capítulo 6: Vivo morrendo
chapters.synopsis: Os amigos encontram um poema com paradoxos e discutem a diferença entre antítese e paradoxo.
chapters.text:
Faltavam poucas páginas para terminarem a leitura do caderno, e os três amigos já tinham criado um ritual: chegavam ao museu às duas da tarde, a tia servia suco de cajá, e eles liam um poema novo em voz alta, cada um uma estrofe.
Naquele dia, o poema era curto e estranho:
"Vivo morrendo, e morro sem morrer;
É doce a dor que a alma me consola;
Prendo-me livre, livre me faz prender
A fé que tudo dá e tudo rola."
— Esse aí deu nó no meu cérebro — confessou Tomás.
— Como alguém vive morrendo? — perguntou Bia. — E como uma dor pode ser doce?
Lia sorriu, porque sentia que finalmente sabia uma resposta.
— Não é para entender ao pé da letra. É um paradoxo.
— Qual é a diferença entre paradoxo e antítese? — quis saber Tomás, puxando um papel, como sempre.
A tia Celeste sentou-se com eles.
— Na antítese, as ideias opostas aparecem lado a lado, mas cada uma no seu lugar: "luz e sombra", "ri e chora". No paradoxo, as ideias opostas se juntam numa mesma afirmação, que parece impossível ou absurda: "vivo morrendo", "doce dor". O paradoxo obriga o leitor a parar e pensar num sentido mais profundo.
Tomás escreveu no papel: "Antítese: opostos lado a lado. Paradoxo: opostos fundidos."
— E qual seria esse sentido mais profundo aqui? — perguntou ele.
Ficaram em silêncio. Foi Bia quem arriscou:
— Talvez ele queira dizer que cada dia vivido é também um dia a menos. Então viver é ir morrendo um pouco. É triste, mas é verdade.
— E a "doce dor"? — perguntou Lia.
— Pode ser a dor de quem está arrependido, mas sente alívio por ter fé — sugeriu a tia. — Para o homem barroco, o sofrimento podia ser um caminho para a salvação. Por isso ele é doce.
Tomás ficou olhando para o verso "prendo-me livre". Depois falou, meio sem graça:
— Às vezes eu me sinto assim. Tipo, quando eu decido estudar em vez de sair, eu me prendo, mas me sinto livre porque escolhi.
As duas meninas olharam para ele, surpresas. Tomás, que no primeiro dia não entendia poema nenhum, tinha acabado de explicar um paradoxo com a própria vida.
— Viu? — disse Celeste. — A literatura barroca fala de conflitos que continuam existindo. As palavras são antigas, mas os sentimentos são bem conhecidos.
No fim da tarde, eles perceberam que só restava uma página do caderno em branco antes da rosa e da frase "Para quem chegar depois". Lia passou o dedo sobre o papel vazio, sem tocar de verdade.
— E se ele deixou essa página em branco de propósito? — perguntou.
— Para quê? — quis saber Bia.
Lia não respondeu. Mas uma ideia começou a crescer dentro dela, e ela passou a noite inteira escrevendo e apagando versos no caderno da escola.

chapters.title: Capítulo 7: Para quem chegar depois
chapters.synopsis: Na exposição sobre o caderno, Lia apresenta um poema barroco que ela mesma escreveu, respondendo ao frei três séculos depois.
chapters.text:
O museu decidiu organizar uma pequena exposição sobre o caderno de Frei Anselmo do Desterro, e a tia Celeste convidou os três amigos para ajudar. Em duas semanas, a sala do térreo se transformou.
Bia fez os painéis: de um lado, desenhos de rosas vivas e murchas; do outro, um pôr do sol em laranja e roxo, com o poema da "rubra coroa" escrito por cima, em letras cheias de voltas. Tomás preparou um cartaz chamado "Cultismo x Conceptismo", com setas, quadros e exemplos, e até o seu "sermão do celular", que os visitantes adoravam ler. Lia escreveu os textos que explicavam o contexto: o século XVII, a Contrarreforma, a arte que queria emocionar, o homem dividido entre o céu e a terra.
No dia da abertura, a sala ficou cheia. Havia estudantes, turistas, vizinhos curiosos e até uma senhora que disse ter rezado a vida inteira na igreja do outro lado da rua.
Celeste fez um discurso curto e, no final, olhou para a sobrinha.
— A Lia tem uma surpresa.
Lia sentiu as pernas tremerem. Subiu num banquinho, abriu o caderno da escola e explicou:
— Na última página do caderno do frei tem uma frase: "Para quem chegar depois". E antes dela tem uma página em branco. Eu não sei se ele deixou essa página de propósito. Mas eu resolvi imaginar que sim. Então escrevi uma resposta.
E leu:
"Frei, que em sombra e luz te dividias,
Chego depois, mas trago o mesmo peito:
Quero o céu e da terra não me aceito
Longe, e morro de vida em meus dias.
Tua rosa secou, mas não morrias:
Viveste em cada verso, em cada jeito
De ver que o tempo, sendo areia e leito,
Nos foge e fica em tudo o que escrevias."
Por um segundo, ninguém disse nada. Depois a sala aplaudiu tanto que Lia quase caiu do banquinho.
Mais tarde, quando os visitantes já tinham ido embora, os três amigos ficaram sentados no chão da sala vazia.
— Você usou tudo — disse Tomás, contando nos dedos. — Antítese, paradoxo, a areia do sermão, a rosa...
— E até um hipérbato — completou Bia. — "Da terra não me aceito longe."
Lia riu. Não tinha planejado cada figura; elas tinham simplesmente aparecido, como se o frei tivesse ensinado sem dizer nada.
A tia se aproximou com o caderno antigo. Com permissão do museu, ela fez algo que deixou Lia sem palavras: colocou uma cópia do poema dela, impressa num papel especial, na página em branco, logo antes da rosa.
— Agora a mensagem tem resposta — disse Celeste.
Naquela noite, Lia voltou para casa a pé de novo, pela orla. As férias estavam acabando, e ela não tinha ido à praia quase nenhum dia. Mesmo assim, achou que tinham sido as melhores férias da vida dela.
Antes de dormir, escreveu no celular, logo abaixo da frase que tinha escrito no primeiro dia: "Entendi o frei. Ele também queria que alguém chegasse depois." E apagou a luz, sem medo do escuro.

books.title: The River and the Harbour
books.premise: Sixteen-year-old Noor must write a coursework essay comparing a play and a novella. Episode by episode, with her friend Theo and her grandmother, she learns to read stage directions, question a narrator, structure a comparison, spot dramatic irony and weave evidence into an argument.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Two Texts on a Desk
chapters.synopsis: Noor must choose two texts for her coursework comparison and, after a rainy afternoon in the library, finds an unexpected pair.
chapters.text:
The rain had been falling on the library windows since lunch, steady and grey, like someone patiently tapping a pencil. Noor Haddad sat at the long table by the radiator with two piles of books and a coursework task sheet that she had read so many times the corners had gone soft.
"Compare two complete texts, one of which must be a drama," it said. "About one thousand five hundred words."
On the left pile were plays. On the right pile were novels and novellas. Noor had already rejected six of them. One play was too long, one novel was too sad, and one she simply did not understand.
Her friend Theo dropped into the chair opposite, shaking water from his hood like a dog. "Still choosing?" he asked.
"Still choosing," Noor said. "Ms Varga says the best comparisons are between texts that are having a conversation, even if their writers never met."
Theo picked up a thin play from the left pile. It was called The Ferryman's Tide, and the cover showed a small boat on a black river. "This one's short," he said hopefully.
Noor took it and began to read the opening stage directions aloud. "A jetty at dusk. The water is never still. EDDA, an old ferrywoman, coils a rope as if it were a sleeping animal." She stopped. Something about the rope and the restless water made her think of another book.
She reached into the right pile and pulled out Glass Harbour, a novella she had read in the summer. It told the story of a girl named Ilse who grew up in a harbour town and wanted, more than anything, to leave it.
"Listen," Noor said, opening it near the beginning. "'The sea kept its promises to no one, and still the town waited for it every morning.'"
Theo frowned. "So they both have water in them. Lots of books have water in them."
"No, it's more than that," Noor said slowly. "In both of them, the sea is a kind of character. It's the thing that keeps people in place and the thing that could take them away. Edda can't leave her river. Ilse can't stop thinking about leaving her harbour."
She wrote two words at the top of a clean page: staying and leaving. Then, underneath, she drew a line down the middle and wrote a title on each side.
By the time the rain stopped, Noor had filled half the page with quick notes. It was not an essay yet. It was barely a plan. But when she packed her bag, she felt, for the first time that week, that the two books on her desk were talking to each other, and that she might be able to listen.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Reading Between the Stage Directions
chapters.synopsis: In a drama lesson, Noor discovers that stage directions in a play can do some of the work that a narrator does in a novel.
chapters.text:
On Tuesday, Ms Varga pushed the desks to the walls and handed out copies of the first scene of The Ferryman's Tide. "We are not going to read this," she announced. "We are going to stand it up."
Noor was given the part of Edda. Theo, who had not volunteered, was given the part of Jory, a young traveller who arrives at the jetty and asks to be taken across the river.
"Before anyone speaks," said Ms Varga, "read the stage directions. In a novel, a narrator can tell you what a character is thinking. In a play, you only get what people say and what they do. So the stage directions matter enormously."
Noor read them again. Edda coils a rope as if it were a sleeping animal. She does not look up when Jory enters. Later, when Jory offers her money, she pauses for a long time before she takes it.
"Why does she pause?" asked Ms Varga.
"Because she doesn't want to go?" Theo guessed.
"Or because she's been asked that question too many times," Noor said. "She's tired of carrying people to the other side when she never goes there herself."
Ms Varga smiled. "Show me."
So Noor tried it. She knelt on the classroom floor with an imaginary rope, kept her eyes down when Theo approached, and let the silence stretch before she held out her hand. The class went quiet. For a moment the classroom really did feel like a jetty at dusk.
Afterwards, Noor opened Glass Harbour at the chapter where Ilse's father refuses to let her take the ferry to the city. The novelist does not leave anything to the reader's imagination. Ilse tells us exactly what she feels: "I hated him for loving me so carefully."
Noor wrote in her notebook: In the novella, the narrator explains the feeling directly. In the play, the silence and the pause make the audience feel it for themselves.
"That's a comparison," Ms Varga said, reading over her shoulder. "Not a list of things that are the same, but a point about how two writers use different tools to reach a similar effect."
On the way out, Theo admitted he had quite enjoyed being Jory. "Although," he added, "I still don't know whether he ever gets across the river."
"Neither do I," said Noor. "We haven't read that far yet."
She tucked the script into her bag carefully, the way Edda had held her rope, as though something inside it might wake up.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Voice in the Harbour
chapters.synopsis: Noor rereads Glass Harbour and realises that its first-person narrator is not as reliable as she first believed.
chapters.text:
On Saturday morning, Noor's grandmother found her at the kitchen table surrounded by sticky notes of five different colours.
"Are you building something?" her grandmother asked, putting down a plate of warm bread.
"An argument," Noor said. "Or I'm trying to."
She was rereading Glass Harbour, and something was bothering her. The first time she had read it, she had trusted Ilse completely. Ilse told the story, so Noor had believed every word. Ilse said the town was cruel, so the town was cruel. Ilse said her father was a coward, so he was a coward.
But this time, Noor noticed small moments that did not fit. In chapter four, Ilse says nobody ever helped her family, yet two pages later a neighbour brings fish to the door every Friday. In chapter six, Ilse calls her father a coward, but the same chapter mentions, almost by accident, that he once rowed out in a storm to rescue a stranded boy.
Noor marked these moments with orange notes. Orange was for doubt.
"Grandma," she said, "if someone tells you their own story, can you believe them?"
Her grandmother laughed. "You can believe that it's their story. That's not always the same as believing it's the whole story."
Noor wrote that down, word for word, and then crossed it out because it was not her own sentence. Instead she wrote: Ilse is a first-person narrator whose anger shapes what she notices. The reader is invited to see more than she can.
Then she picked up The Ferryman's Tide. In a play there was no narrator at all, so nobody could steer the audience in the same way. The audience saw Edda and Jory from the outside, at the same distance, and had to judge them both.
"That's interesting," Noor murmured. "In the novella, I have to look past the narrator to find the truth. In the play, I have to look past the dialogue, because the characters don't say what they mean."
She stuck a green note, for connections, between the two books.
Her grandmother read the note upside down. "You know," she said, "your grandfather never said 'I love you' either. He just fixed the gate every time it broke."
Noor looked up. It was exactly the kind of thing that happened in both texts: love hidden inside small, practical actions. She added another green note and decided that, when the essay was finished, her grandmother would be the first person to read it.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Argument in the Corridor
chapters.synopsis: Noor and Theo disagree about whether Noor's essay should go through the texts one at a time or compare them point by point.
chapters.text:
By Wednesday, Noor had a plan, and Theo did not like it.
They were waiting outside the science lab, and Noor had shown him the page in her notebook. It was divided into two halves. The first half said Glass Harbour. The second half said The Ferryman's Tide.
"So you'll write about one book," Theo said, "and then the other book?"
"Yes. It's tidy."
"It's two essays stapled together," he said. "Ms Varga said the texts had to be having a conversation. In your plan, the first one finishes talking before the second one even arrives."
Noor felt her face go warm. She hated being wrong, and she especially hated being wrong in a corridor. "Fine," she said. "Then how would you do it?"
Theo took her pencil, which she also hated, and drew three boxes across the page instead of two down it. In the first box he wrote place as a trap. In the second he wrote love shown through actions. In the third he wrote the ending: who leaves?
"Each paragraph is about one idea," he said, "and both texts are in every paragraph. You say what the novella does, then what the play does, then why the difference matters."
Noor stared at the boxes. They were messy, but they were also right, and she knew it.
"You'd need linking words," she said slowly. "Similarly. In contrast. Whereas. Both writers. And the evidence has to be woven in, not dumped at the end like shopping."
"Exactly," Theo said, although he looked surprised that he had agreed with something so organised.
That evening, Noor tried writing the first paragraph. Her first attempt was clumsy: In Glass Harbour the sea is a trap. Also in The Ferryman's Tide the river is a trap. She deleted it.
Her second attempt was better. Both writers present water as something that holds their characters in place, but whereas Ilse describes the sea as a jailer, "keeping its promises to no one", Edda's river is presented through her actions, as she "coils a rope as if it were a sleeping animal", suggesting a trap she has learned to live beside rather than one she fights.
She read it aloud to her bedroom wall. The quotations were short and they sat inside her own sentence instead of standing apart from it. The comparison happened in the middle of the sentence, at the word whereas.
The next morning she found Theo at his locker. "You were right," she said. "Don't get used to it."
"I'll try not to," said Theo, grinning.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Dramatic Irony at the Dress Rehearsal
chapters.synopsis: When the drama club rehearses the final scenes, Noor notices that the audience knows something the characters do not.
chapters.text:
The drama club was staging The Ferryman's Tide for the end-of-term show, and Ms Varga had asked Noor's English class to watch the dress rehearsal. "You will understand a play differently when it is lit," she promised.
The hall smelled of dust and fresh paint. Someone had built a jetty out of old pallets, and a blue cloth rippled across the floor of the stage, moved by two Year 8 students lying hidden underneath it. It was surprisingly convincing.
Noor sat in the third row with her notebook open. This time she was not reading the play; she was watching it happen.
In the second act, there was a moment she had skimmed past on the page. Jory tells Edda that he is travelling to the far bank to find his mother, who left the village years ago. He does not know her name, only that she once worked the ferry. Edda listens with her back to him. The stage direction, which Noor knew by heart, said: She stops coiling the rope. Her hands do not move again until the end of the scene.
In the rehearsal, the actor playing Edda turned slightly towards the audience as she stopped, so that everyone in the hall could see her face but Jory could not.
Noor's pencil froze. The audience understood, at that moment, that Edda might be the mother Jory was looking for. Jory did not understand. Perhaps Edda did not fully understand either.
"Dramatic irony," Theo whispered from the seat beside her.
"Yes," Noor whispered back. "But look at what it does. It makes every line after this hurt more."
She thought about Glass Harbour. The novella did something similar, but the other way round. Because Ilse narrated the story, readers knew only what Ilse knew, and the truth about her father's bravery came out slowly, by accident, in details she did not seem to value. In the novella the irony was hidden inside the narrator's voice. In the play it was placed in the space between the stage and the seats.
After the rehearsal, Noor wrote quickly while the idea was still warm: Both writers create a gap between what a character knows and what the audience or reader knows. In the play, this gap is staged and public; in the novella, it is private and discovered gradually.
On the way out, the two Year 8 students crawled out from under the blue cloth, red-faced and laughing.
"Was the river all right?" one of them asked.
"The river," said Noor, "was perfect."

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The Paragraph That Would Not Work
chapters.synopsis: Halfway through her draft, Noor gets stuck on a paragraph about endings, until a conversation at the bus stop helps her find a sharper argument.
chapters.text:
Noor's draft had reached one thousand and ninety words, and it had stopped there for two days.
The problem was the ending paragraph. Everything else had found its shape. Her paragraphs on place, on hidden love and on dramatic irony each moved between the two texts, with short quotations stitched into her sentences. But the endings refused to fit.
At the end of Glass Harbour, Ilse finally boards the ferry to the city. The last sentence is: "I did not look back, because I knew that if I did, the harbour would look back at me." At the end of The Ferryman's Tide, Jory reaches the far bank, but Edda stays on the jetty, coiling her rope as the lights fade.
"One character leaves and one stays," Noor said to Theo at the bus stop. "So they're just different. That's not an argument. It's a fact."
Theo thought about it while a bus that was not theirs went past. "Does Ilse really leave, though?" he asked eventually. "She says she doesn't look back because the harbour would look back. So the harbour's still in her head."
Noor turned to look at him.
"And Edda stays," Theo went on, "but she's the one who let Jory go. Maybe staying is her way of being brave."
For a second, Noor could not speak. Then she sat down on the cold bench, opened her notebook on her knees and began writing so fast that her handwriting slanted like rain.
Her new paragraph did not say that one character leaves and one stays. It said that both writers question whether leaving and staying are really opposites. Ilse escapes physically, but the novella's final image suggests that the harbour has travelled with her. Edda remains physically, but by carrying Jory across, she frees someone else. The ending of the novella is spoken by a single voice looking forward; the ending of the play is silent and visual, and the audience is left watching a woman who has chosen her place.
She checked her evidence. Two short quotations, one stage direction, and a comment on the effect of each. She checked her linking words: both, whereas, by contrast. She checked that she had not simply retold the stories. She had not.
"Our bus," Theo said, nudging her.
Noor stood up and nearly dropped her notebook. "Thank you," she said. "You changed my whole conclusion."
"I just asked a question," said Theo.
"That," said Noor, climbing the steps of the bus, "is usually how it starts."

chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Grandmother's Verdict
chapters.synopsis: Noor finishes her draft, checks it against the task, and keeps a promise to let her grandmother read it first.
chapters.text:
On Sunday evening, Noor printed her draft. It was one thousand four hundred and eighty words long, and the pages were still warm from the printer when she carried them into the kitchen.
Before she handed it over, she sat down and checked it against the task sheet one last time, the way Ms Varga had taught the class. Two complete texts, one of them a drama: yes. A clear line of argument from the first paragraph to the last: yes, she thought. Every paragraph compared both texts, rather than dealing with them one at a time. Quotations were short and built into her own sentences. She had written about how the writers created effects, not just what happened. And she had remembered that one text was written to be performed, so she had written about the audience, the staging and the silences, not only the words on the page.
There was one sentence she was unsure about, so she read it aloud quietly: "Both writers suggest that a place can live inside a person long after the person has left it." It sounded true. More importantly, she could point to the evidence that made it true.
Her grandmother put on her reading glasses and read slowly, the way she read letters, with a finger resting under each line. Noor tried not to watch. She washed two cups that were already clean. She rearranged the fruit bowl.
At last her grandmother put the pages down.
"I have not read these books," she said. "But now I feel as if I have met the old woman with the rope, and the girl who wanted to leave."
Noor let out a breath she had not noticed she was holding.
"And this part," her grandmother continued, tapping the page about hidden love, "about people who show love by fixing things instead of saying it. You wrote about the books, but I think you were also writing about your grandfather."
"Maybe a little," Noor admitted.
"Good essays usually are a little about the writer," said her grandmother. "Just not too much."
On Monday, Noor handed the draft to Ms Varga, who flicked through it and paused at the conclusion. She did not say anything, but she underlined one sentence and drew a small tick beside it.
After class, Theo asked which sentence it was.
"The one about whether staying and leaving are really opposites," Noor said.
"My idea," Theo said.
"Our idea," said Noor. "That's what a conversation is."
Outside, it had started to rain again, steady and grey, tapping on the windows like a patient pencil. This time, Noor did not mind at all.
